I am 55 years old and have been farming in Quzhou County my whole life. My family has 7 mu of good flat land, all irrigated by well water. I finished middle school, which is enough to read fertilizer bags and follow the county extension office's guidance, but I do not experiment much. I stick with what works.

It is mid-April now, so my winter wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October after rotary tillage. I always plant *luyuan502*, an improved variety that gives steady yields and resists lodging. Right now the wheat is at the jointing stage, so this month I will apply the spring top-dressing: about 45 kg of urea per mu on top of the 100 kg of compound fertilizer (18-22-5) I put down at sowing. That gives me roughly 36 kg of nitrogen, 22 kg of phosphorus, and 7–8 kg of potassium per mu for the wheat crop. I will irrigate three times before harvest in early June — once now at jointing, once at booting, and once at grain filling. I also spray insecticide twice, herbicide once, and fungicide once because the damp spring weather brings aphids and powdery mildew. I expect about 1,000 kg per mu if the weather holds.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. Everyone here uses no-tillage for maize — we cut the wheat straw and sow directly into the stubble. I buy *denghai605*, a hybrid seed, one package per mu. At sowing I apply 80 kg of compound fertilizer (28-6-6) per mu, giving about 22 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate twice: once right after sowing if it is dry, and once at the big-flare stage. I spray insecticide twice and herbicide once; I skip fungicide on maize unless I see rust. With good summer sun, I expect 1,100 kg per mu.

I do not grow cotton or vegetables. The wheat-maize rotation is reliable, the dealers deliver seeds and chemicals to the village, and I can sell both crops to the grain station without worry.
